statement: In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is 4 : 7. There are 9 more girls than boys. How many children are in the class?

choices.misconception: I found the number of boys instead of the whole class.
I added the 9 extra girls to the 11 parts of the ratio.
I found the number of girls instead of the whole class.
I took the 9 extra girls to be one part, so I multiplied 9 by 11.

hints: Draw the boys as 4 equal bars and the girls as 7 bars that size.
The girls have 3 more parts than the boys. Those 3 parts are the 9 extra girls, which tells you the size of one part.
One part is 9 / 3 = 3 children, and the whole class is 4 + 7 = 11 parts.

solutions.reliable: Think of the class as equal parts: boys 4 parts, girls 7 parts. The girls have 7 - 4 = 3 parts more, and that difference is 9 children, so one part is 3 children. The class is 11 parts, so it has 11 x 3 = 33 children. Check: 12 boys and 21 girls give 12 : 21 = 4 : 7, and 21 - 12 = 9. The transferable idea: match the difference you are given to the difference in parts to find the size of one part.

whyOnTest: Ratio-as-parts questions test matching a given number to the right number of parts, then scaling to the part you need.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
